newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FORECAST-Australian jobs market still in stalemate.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Australian jobs market still in stalemate.

text.p: The picture of Australia's labour force in February is expected to be little changed from that of recent times -- one of employment growing, but not fast enough to make any inroads into the unemployment rate.
Thursday's data is expected to show that employment remained subdued in early 1997, although there is some increased optimism among economists of moderate strength later in the year.
The median forecast of the 28 economists Reuters surveyed was for a 13,500 rise in employment and an unemployment rate of 8.7 percent.

That series pointed to jobs growth of around 15,000 a month over the June quarter, insufficient to meet the government's forecast of 1.5 percent employment growth in 1996/97 (July-June), ANZ chief economist Saul Eslake said.
However, the trend series was still rising, "consistent with the notion that a modest recovery in the demand for labour is now underway," Eslake said.
If the recent script on the labour market was to change, the risks were for a stronger number after the distortions to the series caused by a new telephone survey method.

Initially, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said the new method was having no detectable impact. Then in January, it said the new method appeared to be underestimating employment growth by between 6,000 and 9,000 a month.

Finally in March, when the February data was released, the ABS said that the early understatement had itself been reversed by an overstatement of employment growth over the later months of the implementation period.
If growth was overstated in the past few months, it would mean that the fall in February employment was actually closer to 20,000, Bankers Trust senior economist David Bassanese said.

"With the level of job vacancies suggesting employment growth should be at least 10,000 to 15,000 per month, a large positive correction should be expected in March," he said, forecasting a 25,000 rise in the month.

Commonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney also expected a 25,000 increase. He said employment growth was under the levels indicated by job vacancies, and there were indications employers had not acted to fill all vacancies creating some pent up demand for labour.
"This raises the possibility of a snapback in employment growth at some stage," Moloney said.
Looking further ahead, there were other signs that employment prospects would improve through 1997, with signs of pick up in both the housing and retailing sectors becoming apparent.
As employment is a lagging indicator of activity, labour demand should pick up later this year given the signs of strength begining to be seen in the economy, economists said.
However, the pace of economic recovery and jobs growth is expected to be moderate, leaving the unemployment rate above eight percent for at least most of the year.

"The key information here is that, although the job ads series suggests that the outlook for the labour market is improving, the pickup is fairly subdued in nature," ANZ Securities economists said after Monday's release of the job advertisement series. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
